newsitem.title: USA: Daschle says tax deal possible by end of week.
newsitem.headline: Daschle says tax deal possible by end of week.

text.p: Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle left open the possibility on Saturday that the White House and Congress could agree on a tax-cutting plan by the end of the week, but said he would urge a veto if the Senate's current plan remained intact.
"I think there's a possibility we could complete it," he said on CNN's "Evans & Novak" programme. "We're working this weekend. We'll be working all days next week."

Negotiators for the Clinton administration and the Republican-controlled House and Senate were meeting over the weekend in an effort to resolve differences between the three different tax plans that would be part of the May budget deal between Congress and Clinton that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.
Previously, the South Dakota Democrat had been less upbeat about the prospects for a deal, saying the July 25 deadline that Republican congressional leaders had imposed on themselves was too short.

But Daschle said he would urge President Clinton to veto the final tax plan if it were the same as the one the Senate passed on June 27, saying it doesn't address "the principles" outlined in the deal between the Congress and the White House, including $35 billion in tax breaks for higher education expenses.
"We want to find more fairness in the tax code then what this bill offers," he said.
The bill drew 80 of the Senate's 100 votes, including Daschle's, who said he voted for it only so that it could be moved along and reconciled with the House version and administration proposals.

One difference is over capital gains taxes, with the Republicans offering a deeper cut than Democrats. Daschle said, however, that he would not recommend a presidential veto solely over differences over a capital gains tax cut.

Daschle cited four key elements that he said must be in a final tax package, including making low-income taxpayers who qualify for earned income tax credits eligibilty to receive the $500 per child tax credit, which Republicans oppose.

He said a final tax-cutting bill also must have "more fiscal responsibility" to keep the budget deficit from explosding in later years, a full $35 billion in tax breaks for higher education and more "budget investments" and aid to urban areas.
